https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ev: Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.
The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.
A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.
About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.
The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support .

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.
Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".
The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.
Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth"
Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq: Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature

A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
As Europe sees a wave of cyber-attacks on commercial fridges, we investigate how everyday devices are vulnerable to basic attacks using easily-available tools.
The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3x2: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4g: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is selling shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $81bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta from StoneX trading.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.
McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'
Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6e9: There were 22 people on board the Bayesian at the time of the incident

The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about critical safety risks that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily, killing seven people, British investigators say.
British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024.

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.
Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.
"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

The accident also led to the deaths of Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71; American lawyer Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57; and crew member Rick Thomas , 59.
Mike Lynch and his daughter Hannah both died when the Bayesian sank

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."
Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184ft) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.
The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".
In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.
In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.
With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).
The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.
The wreckage of the Bayesian off the coast of Porticello, Sicily

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.
Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.
They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.
The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.
Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.
As it heeled over, five people were injured, either by falling or by items falling on them and a deckhand was thrown into the sea, the report said.

As water started entering the yacht, two of the guests "used the furniture drawers as an improvised ladder to exit into the central alleyway", then climbed along the internal walls to get into the saloon.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckq6: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c674: Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.

From the memes to the music - from the controversies to the culture - you have your say on GTA 6 with Newsbeat's Jordan Kenny and De-Graft Mensah.

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.
Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".
The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm9q: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
Democrats won Congress in a blue wave. Now comes the hard part.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmd7: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.
At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) with director of football Jason Wilcox
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".
"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."
United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.
Andrey Santos has started four Premier League games for Manchester United since his £50m summer move from Chelsea

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.

Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.
"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: There is a string of symbols tattooed on to Will Stuart's left foot.
A circle, two triangles, an up arrow, another circle, R1, L2, an up arrow, a triangle, and, finally L1 three times.
England and British and Irish Lions star Stuart is indelibly, if jokingly, stamped with a Grand Theft Auto cheat code, , external which gives your character maximum in-game sex appeal.

So far, this autumn, that objective has been achieved. Twickenham has been seduced by two charismatic displays which have been high on entertainment, if low on jeopardy.
New Zealand are sore. Last weekend's defeat by Wales - their first in 73 years - stung. Coach Dave Rennie's public accusation that the players had "let the country down" will have salted wounds.
He may well have said the same of the insipid performance the team put up in a 33-19 defeat by England last year, under his predecessor Scott Robertson.

Despite last week's reverse, New Zealand - along with world champions South Africa - are where southern-hemisphere quality is concentrated. And where England's revival will be truly stress-tested.
The comeback of Stuart, and others, has been key for England.
England made a clean sweep of their last autumn campaign, with a high-calibre set of replacements key.
Any lingering final-quarter hopes for the visitors were flushed out by England's depth on the bench.

George Martin - an old-school second row enforcer who is recently back from his own 14-month lay-off - is on a bench, also including Henry Pollock and Marcus Smith, loaded with stardust and points to prove.
George Furbank, whose running threat and playmaking ability from deep adds an extra dimension to attack, starts at full-back after a rotten run of knocks and set-backs.

Captain Maro Itoje seems rejuvenated by a summer off. Ollie Chessum is perhaps in the best form of his life. Seb Atkinson - still only eight caps into his Test career - has brought a mix of hard running and soft skills to 12.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Andoni Iraola's Liverpool take on Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on Sunday

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.
Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.
The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.
Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.
"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.
"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."
Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.
"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."
Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.
"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.
"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."
Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.
But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.
"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.
"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.
"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

A ruthless Carlos Alcaraz put aside his injury concerns to dismantle Flavio Cobolli and ensure a perfect record in the ATP Finals group stages.
Spain's Alcaraz hurt his left hamstring in his previous match against Daniil Medvedev and had a scan on the injury on Thursday.
He arrived for his match against Cobolli with strapping on his upper-left leg - as well as tape on his right knee and a sleeve on his right arm - but was brutally efficient in a 6-4 6-1 win.
The seven-time Grand Slam champion did not face a break point and bludgeoned 29 winners in a 65-minute victory.
"I tried not to move that much. I tried to be aggressive, to dominate the match as much as I can," the 23-year-old said.
"I'm just really happy that I am getting more confident, the way I'm hitting the ball and seeing what's going on in the match.
"The challenge now is not on the court, it's off the court, to do whatever it takes to be in a good shape and feel physically ready for a battle tomorrow."
Alcaraz is now on a 12-match winning streak and will face Ben Shelton, who he beat in the Paris Masters final last month, in Saturday's semi-finals.
The winner of Friday's last match between Medvedev and Frances Tiafoe will face Alexander Zverev in the other semi-final.
Alcaraz was conservative in his movement, trying to avoid sliding in and out of the corners - but rather than diminishing his game, it allowed him to produce some astonishing shot-making.
Cobolli never looked as though he had the belief that he could challenge Alcaraz, and was broken in the first game of the match by a thumping return winner.
Alcaraz kept the points short, hammering his forehand and backhand to all corners, and targeted Cobolli's second serve in particular.
An astonishing whipped 110mph forehand winner was the highlight of the first set, which Alcaraz wrapped up with a strong service hold.
Cobolli again lost his serve in the opening game of the second set and Alcaraz claimed five of the final six games to secure victory.
After converting match point with another return winner, Alcaraz embraced Cobolli at the net and offered the crushed Italian a few words of support.
Alcaraz has not had his serve broken once in his three group matches as he bids for a first title at the season-ending event.
He and world number one Zverev have both made it through the group stages without dropping a set, while Alcaraz has not lost more than four games in a set.
In the doubles, Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison reached the semi-finals with a 7-6 (7-5) 6-4 victory over Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Joao Pedro has scored five goals in six Premier League games this season
Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.
The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland , the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.

The 25-year-old will miss Leeds United 's visit on Saturday with a thigh injury after Chelsea lost three of their previous four matches without him, although one defeat came in a penalty shootout against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

Having suffered a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham in that run, manager Xabi Alonso has faced criticism over his side's lack of identity and some of his personnel decisions , particularly when attempting to replace Joao Pedro.
Danny Welbeck, who was expected to provide cover after his summer arrival from Brighton , has started only one Premier League match during Joao Pedro's injury absence.

Instead, Pedro Neto has twice been deployed through the middle, in the home win over Manchester United and the defeat by Sunderland , while Morgan Rogers started as the central striker against Spurs .
Striker Emmanuel Emegha, signed from Strasbourg over the summer, hasn't started a league game but has struggled with fitness issues of his own.
The continued absence of Joao Pedro is certainly proving costly before the busy winter schedule, with fifth-placed Chelsea already 11 points behind Premier League leaders Arsenal .
Having been handed both a new contract until 2034 and the number nine shirt vacated by Liam Delap in August, Chelsea regard their £55m signing from Brighton in 2025 as a key figure in Alonso's plans.

Asked about scoring more goals without the striker on Friday, Alonso said: "Yes, we need the whole team for that. It's not just the strikers who can score, we can score in set-pieces from defenders, midfielders, so it's teamwork for sure.

"Joao is an important player but we need to be this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.
"The other players, they need to step up and they need to show that they are ready to compete and ready to play for Chelsea ."
There is little doubt Alonso has suffered when Joao Pedro has been unavailable, as did his predecessors. The numbers are undeniable.
Since the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, Chelsea have averaged 1.8 goals per game with Joao Pedro, compared to 0.6 without.
Their expected goals (xG) drop from 1.8 per game with him to 1.1 without, highlighting a decline in Chelsea's attacking output rather than simply their finishing.
Chelsea average 4.8 shots on target per game when the Brazilian plays, compared with 3.9 when he does not.
Chelsea have failed to score in only 12.2% of Premier League matches involving him, compared with 71.4% when he has been absent.

Chelsea have lost without scoring in just 7.3% of league games featuring Joao Pedro, compared with 71.4% without him. Three of their Premier League defeats this season were without him, while they have scored in every game that he has featured.
Chelsea's points-per-game average falls from 1.5 to 0.9 when he is unavailable.
Joao Pedro, who has also operated as a number 10 and on the wing for Chelsea , appears to improve the output of those around him.
During the past season and a half, Palmer has played 2,317 Premier League minutes alongside him and 528 without him.

Palmer has scored 12 goals and registered four assists with the Brazil forward in the side, equating to 0.6 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Without him, Palmer has managed one goal and no assists, equivalent to 0.2 goal involvements per 90.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic: Leon Smith was Andy Murray's childhood coach before taking over as Britain's Davis Cup captain in 2010
Great Britain's Davis Cup-winning captain Leon Smith says it is the "right time" to leave the role after almost 17 years - although Andy Murray is not ready to replace him.
Smith was appointed in 2010 and guided the British men's team to Davis Cup victory in 2015 - the nation's first win in the event since 1936.
The 50-year-old Scot's successor has not yet been appointed, but the Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) has spoken to potential candidates and hopes to announce the new captain as soon as possible.
Former world number one Murray, who was instrumental in Britain's 2015 triumph, is not believed to be interested in the role at this stage.
Since retiring in 2024, Murray has been enjoying spending more time with his family and working on business interests, as well as coaching Novak Djokovic and now Jack Draper on a part-time basis.
"He obviously is the standout candidate, isn't he?" said Smith.
"I do hope it's something he does in the future, but I respect that it's not for him right now, and I can understand it.
"But I really hope at some point in the future that he does take it on."
Smith said he had been pondering his future for "most of this year" before deciding to step down after next week's Finals in Bologna.
"There comes a time whether it is personally you need a change, or it is good for the team to have something else," said Smith, who seemed emotional in a video call with reporters.
Leon Smith guided Great Britain to their first Davis Cup title in 79 years
"I've done it for a very long time and I think there are others who will enjoy the role and can bring something different to the role.
"I love the role and haven't lost any passion for it. But it feels like the right time for me personally and the guys moving forwards."
With Smith picking the team and creating a tight bond between the group, Murray was the driving force on the court as he won all eight of his singles matches in the victorious campaign.
Murray, 39, was coached by Smith as a child and said winning the Davis Cup together was "one of the proudest moments" of his career.
"He did a great job of bringing everyone together and making sure we all felt we had a part to play. He got the best out of us that year," three-time Grand Slam champion Murray said.
"I've obviously known Leon a long time. I think the most fun we had together was when I was playing Davis Cup and Leon was on the bench. I'm really glad we got to share those moments.
"I wish Leon all the best as he steps down, and good luck to the new captain."
Smith, who will continue in his role as head of British men's tennis, took over almost 17 years ago with the team in danger of being relegated to the lowest tier of the Davis Cup.
Within three years they were back in the top tier and just two years later Murray inspired them to the trophy.
Smith also guided the team to the semi-finals in 2016 and 2019.
While he can no longer rely on a superstar of Murray's ilk, Smith is hoping this year's crop can ensure his captaincy ends on another high.

Britain will rely on Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery and former world number eight Cameron Norrie in the singles, with world number one Henry Patten and three-time major champion Neal Skupski pairing up in the doubles.
Smith's side faces Germany - led by singles world number one Alexander Zverev - in the last eight on Thursday.
"I'm focused and really looking forward to captaining Great Britain for one more week in Bologna next week and hopefully creating a few more special memories together," Smith added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/netball/arti: Captain James Thomson-Boston will lead England out to face Jamaica
It's not that men aren't playing it - it's just that you're not seeing it.
That is the message echoed by both James Thomson-Boston - captain of the England men's netball side - and Jamaica defender Authorn Chambers.
These two men's sides have history, and are about to meet again.

In a historic first, their matches will be played as curtain-raisers before England's women, ranked third in the world, face fourth-placed Jamaica in the Vitality Netball Horizon Series in London this weekend.
With an inaugural men's World Cup on the cards, likely within the next few years, BBC Sport looks at the signs that indicate that, if not already, the men's game will soon be on your radar.
A new era for England Roses under Stembridge - watch on the BBC
The narrative of women's sport fighting for recognition in a historically male-dominated space is a familiar one, but in netball - traditionally a female sport - it is quite the opposite.
Yet in recent years, the rise of the men's game has been meteoric.
The England men's team, known as the Thorns - in contrast to the women's Roses - played their first international in October 2022 and are now coached by women's Netball Super League coach Jo Noel.

They have played international Test series against the likes of Australia, toured St Kitts & Nevis for the Americas Netball Men's Championship, and are now set to play Jamaica for the first time on home soil.
Overseas, Australia and New Zealand contest the Trans-Tasman Cup, while African nations play in the Africa Netball Cup.
And now, 63 years after the first women's World Cup, the sport's global governing body, World Netball, says plans are being developed to host an inaugural men's edition.

In a statement to BBC Sport, it said: "World Netball will always remain proud of the sport's unique female-focused foundations; however we are also a sport that is open to all. We should celebrate and be proud of our traditions but not a hostage to them.

"It needs to be in those kind of spaces that people are seeing it - that's how it's going to grow," he said.

Thomson-Boston moved to England from Australia 10 years ago. While searching for a netball club to join, he was asked if he actually meant a football club.

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.
After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.
They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.
The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.
"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.
That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.
So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?
Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.
An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.
However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.
Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).
They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.
Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.
"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.
"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."
This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.
Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.
"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.
"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"
Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007
Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, who had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.
Russell said: "We know in the wet it is different every lap, every session, realistically we were not the fastest today.
"McLaren looked exceptionally fast. Charles looked very fast at points, we just got the lap in when the track was at its driest and Norris didn't run.
"We have some things to understand because Kimi and I were very competitive in the wet last week and both of us were off the pace."
Hadjar added: "It was good fun but I don't think it's very useful for tomorrow. Just shaking down the car."
McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.
New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.
Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.
Perhaps surprisingly given the conditions, the session was incident-free, although it was stopped briefly in the closing stages to recover a plastic bag that had blown on to the circuit.

This issue is exacerbated this year with the new 'straight-line mode', in which the wings open to reduce drag on the straights to aid energy recovery.

Russell said: "It's always a challenge here in Vegas but the added challenge this year with the nature of the cars, the SM zones everywhere, you're not putting any vertical load in the tyres so they are getting substantially cooler in the straight than in the previous years and they were already pretty cool."
In the first practice session, no driver completed a timed lap because the track was extremely wet and teams preferred to save their limited allocation of wet-weather tyres.

Hamilton said: "It wasn't a great day just sitting around waiting. You can't really test much in those conditions. And everything you learn from today you have to forget because tomorrow is supposed to be dry, so we kind of start from tomorrow.
"Everyone is (going in blind). No-one has put the slicks on, so we will have to react quickly. Hopefully, it's not bad and we are there or thereabouts."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2717125: The home of rugby has been a field of mixed fortune for the All Blacks.
While Twickenham has seen some of the side's greatest triumphs, it has also played host to a few of its darkest days.
This weekend could well define Dave Rennie's rookie year, after a shock loss to Wales, his side need to respond against the English at 'Twickers'.
With so much on the line in London, including a place in the first ever Nations Championship final, RNZ takes a look back at the best and worst All Black performances on the hallowed turf.

One of the All Blacks finest hours . A side packed with legends from skipper Richie McCaw, Dan Carter, Ma'a Nonu, Conrad Smith, Keven Mealamu, and Tony Woodcock, playing their final test, closing out the last true era of dominance from the men in black. After a clinical early try for Nehe Milner-Skudder, Nonu scored an individual stunner from halfway, before Carter put things out of reach with a penalty and drop goal. The final nail came as Ben Smith stabbed a kick ahead from his own 22 for Beauden Barrett to fly on to, expertly control, and ground to secure a third World Cup title. Carter capped off the victory with a cheeky right footed conversion, such was the confidence of the '15 side.

Just a week earlier, the All Blacks endured one of their most bruising ever battles with the Boks to secure their place in the final. Despite out-scoring South Africa two tries to none through Milner-Skudder and Jerome Kaino, Handre Pollard kept his side in touch with five penalties, Pat Lambie coming on to nail one of his own to reduce the margin to two. But despite the late Springbok onslaught, the All Black defence held firm, a Ben Franks hit jolting the ball free to end another famous clash between the old rivals.
Richie McCaw and Kieran Read celebrate their semi final win over South Africa.

"It's 1995 all over again," Keith Quinn roared as Jonah Lomu once again rampaged his way through the English defence on the world stage . Having sent them tumbling out of the tournament four years prior with his spectacular quartet in Cape Town, Lomu repeated the dose of damage in their own backyard, steamrolling four English on his way to a fifty metre scorcher. The All Blacks were on fire early after Christian Cullen, controversially playing centre, sliced through the line to set up Jeff Wilson. Johnny Wilkinson kept England in the hunt, but after Lomu broke the 16-all deadlock, the win was sealed when Byron Kelleher sneaked down the blindside to ensure the All Blacks would top Pool B.

The Invincibles left a lasting mark on Europe , including at Twickenham, becoming the first All Blacks side to play at the famous ground and securing the first All Blacks win. A gruelling tour off the field but a flawless one on it, the formidable side arrived at Twickenham having swept their way past 27 opponents for 27 wins, with just five matches remaining on the historic tour. The London leg included three matches at Twickenham, two county games and the third of four tests on tour. The English test is perhaps most remembered for the dramatic sending off of Cyril Brownlie, the first All Black to be given his marching orders. Brother Maurice would respond with one of four All Black tries, as they established a 14-point lead with 14 men, before a late surge from the home side made for a more respectable scoreline. The side would win their final four games on tour to return home with a perfect 32 from 32 record. The result would be the first of six wins on the trot for the All Blacks over England, a run that was finally broken in 1936.

Navajo Stirling will fight former light heavyweight champion Jiří Procházka with potential title implications on the line.
A win over Procházka would make it hard for the UFC to deny him a shot at the belt, currently held by City Kickboxing teammate, Carlos Ulberg.
Meanwhile, Dan Hooker will be hoping to have this hand raised for the first time in over two years and halt a three-fight losing streak when he takes on American Brian Ortega.
The co-main event is a featherweight match-up between former bantamweight champion Aljamain Sterling and rising star Kevin Vallejos.
Flyweights Kyoji Horiguchi and Asu Almabayev, and middleweights Jared Cannonier and Ikram Aliskerov round out the main card.
New Zealand's Carlos Ulberg punches Jiri Prochazka of Czechia in a light heavyweight title bout during UFC 327.

Stirling is coming off a career-best performance against another former light heavyweight champion in Jan Blachowicz.
The 29-year-old earned performance of the night honours with a first-round TKO finish, his third in his last three fights, making him the bookies favourite on Sunday.
A win over Procházka could see Stirling handed a title shot in a division desperate for new talent.
After winning and vacating the belt in 2023 due to injury, Procházka has failed in his last three attempts as the challenger.
The last being against current champion and Kiwi Ulberg, who overcame a leg injury to knock out the unorthodox Czech fighter in the first round at UFC 327 in April.
Stirling's age and novelty as a fresh face puts him in the driver's seat for a title shot with a win over Procházka.
However, it also could present another challenge entirely, a potential clash with teammate Ulberg for the light heavyweight crown.
Stirling has previously said he didn't want to fight Ulberg, and believed he could bide his time with youth on his side.
Stirling - "Prior to UFC I was definitely a fan of Jiri, I knew who he was before the UFC did and here I am fighting him. But at the end of the day, I'm just going to go and smash his face in.

"I can impose my game on anyone, I have so many tools, I can fight forward, I can go back, I can scrap if I want. In this sport, to be a name you have to beat a name."
Having headlined Qatar's UFC debut last year, Hooker returns in hopes of ending his losing streak against former two-time featherweight challenger Ortega.

Beauden Barrett's All Blacks career has taken another remarkable turn, with the veteran playmaker on the verge of a milestone few could have imagined when he was overlooked at the start of the season .
The 35-year-old will become just the fourth player in rugby history to play 150 tests when he runs out at Twickenham on Sunday morning (NZT), having been named to start at fullback against England.
He will be the first back to reach the milestone and only the second All Black to do so. He is also just four tests away from overtaking Sam Whitelock (153) as New Zealand's most-capped player.
All Blacks coach Dave Rennie, who took charge of the team at the start of the season, said it was a remarkable achievement.
"It's a phenomenal feat for a start to bring up 150 tests," Rennie told reporters in London. "He's been a brilliant player for a long time."
Although Rennie has only worked with Barrett for a few months, the coach said the veteran's professionalism and influence had made a lasting impression.
"What I've been most impressed with is the quality of the man he is off-field as well.
"He leads really well. He deeply cares about the jersey and the legacy and is constantly driving that. He's an excellent influence on all our young men coming through the system.
"Fifteen years at this level is phenomenal and to be playing at the quality that he's played and the form that he's in speaks volumes."
Barrett has retained his place in the starting side to face England, with Rennie making eight changes following last weekend's shock loss to Wales .

Several first choice players return to the starting XV , including lock Fabian Holland, loose forward Tupou Vaa'i, hooker and captain Codie Taylor, midfielder Jordie Barrett and star wing Will Jordan, who is back from a hamstring injury earlier than expected.

Jordan, the All Blacks' leading try-scorer with 56 test tries, has seen Barrett's influence first-hand. The pair have played together throughout Jordan's international career, with the younger back crediting Barrett as one of the people who helped shape him as an All Black.
"It's been one of the great privileges of my All Black career, playing with Beaudy and being around him as a team-mate," Jordan said.
"Someone I class as good friend, he was certainly someone who took me under their wing when I first came into the team and he's done that with every player."
Jordan, who will bring up his 65th test on the weekend, said Barrett's longevity was difficult to comprehend.
"One hundred and fifty tests is a crazy feat of longevity," Jordan said.
"I was a reflecting yesterday and it feels like I've been around for a while now and I'm at 65 tests this weekend, so I'm only halfway.
"I've got Damian McKenzie or Jordie Barrett's full test career to go to get to Beaudy's achievement, which seems ridiculous."
Beauden Barrett (centre) looks dejected following the loss to Wales.
Barrett's path to the milestone has not been straightforward.
He was overlooked for the All Blacks' first six tests of the year, with Rennie making it clear the veteran had slipped down the pecking order.
But he has fought his way back into the starting side, starting New Zealand's last four tests and putting himself within touching distance of Whitelock's all-time record.
Jordan said Barrett's achievement was a reflection of his relentless work ethic, and the All Blacks were determined to mark the occasion with a win.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmpd: Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its £500m target.
In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures would be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.
The BBC welcomed the report, saying it had "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".
The NAO report , external also said the BBC's current measures were expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.
Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.
BBC director-general Matt Brittin previously described the licence fee model as a "busted flush"

The NAO noted the BBC's licence fee income had fallen by 26% in real terms over the last decade, in part because of the significant changes in audience habits and successive government freezes in the licence fee.
The proportion of UK adults using BBC television, iPlayer, radio or online services on an average week also fell from 90% in 2021-22 to 81% in 2025-26, the NAO said.
The report noted the corporation's public service broadcasting operating deficit had reached £209m in the last financial year.
The BBC has already announced plans to reduce spending by about 10%, including cuts to programming across its news, nations and content divisions.
Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank, Live At The Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and RuPaul's Drag Race UK are among the TV programmes to have been cut so far.
Radio programmes are also being dropped from the schedules, such as BBC Radio 4's You and Yours, and The World Tonight.
The corporation has also announced plans to close the linear broadcast services of BBC Radio 4 Extra, BBC Three and BBC Scotland, with the latter two becoming online-only services.

The NAO said the BBC expected to face difficult choices about the scale and scope of its services as part of its latest savings programme, with further content reductions expected to have a greater impact on audiences.
It warned the corporation was likely to find it harder to identify further savings following its previous cost-cutting programmes.
The NAO also found the broadcaster had not properly monitored the cumulative impact of its previous savings on audiences, service quality and organisational capability.
It also raised concerns about the BBC's risk management and governance arrangements, and said stronger oversight would be needed to deliver the more demanding savings programme.

In response to the report, the BBC said it welcomed the findings, adding that it had had to "make tough decisions due to sustained financial pressures driven by declining licence fee income, changing audience behaviour, increased competition and rising costs".

Berangere Michel, the BBC's group chief financial officer, said: "We welcome this report and are pleased that the NAO has acknowledged the significant savings already delivered by the BBC, with the programme on track to meet its target one year ahead of schedule.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62: The singer-songwriter from Pontprennau in Cardiff recently sang at the Carnaby Street Christmas lights switch-on in London
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.
In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.
The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.
While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."
His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.
Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.
Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).
Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.
The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.
Before Miller, the last Welsh solo male artist to top the singles chart was Shakin' Stevens with Merry Christmas Everyone
Regardless of the outcome of the Christmas charts, it is clear the success of Babydoll has had an enormous impact on the singer's life.
He previously shared with the BBC that "nothing feels normal" after the success of the track.
The star said Babydoll came after "a really, really hard few years in my personal life" and with almost 10 years of trying to make it in the industry, he had decided to give it one "last chance".
Miller praised his mum, Anne, when he appeared on the podcast The Person Who Believed in Me for her unwavering support.
He said that, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.
But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".
"She's just the best thing that's ever happened to me," Miller said.
Miller lives in Los Angeles and says, no matter the time difference, his mum Anne "will always be there on the end of a phone call"
He also credited Anne for helping him get out of the "dark headspace" he was in some years ago: "There was a point where I didn't want to be here anymore. Being in that mind-frame was really scary."

He said she flew to the United States where he was living to spend time with him, and her love for him, expressed in "going on beach walks, going to grab me a coffee, pulling me out of bed", was what "got him out".
Miller also disclosed that money was something he had worried about throughout his life, adding the moment he knew he had "made it" was when he earned enough to help his parents retire.
The singer said his mum had "served everybody else for so long" and talked excitedly about calling her to say: "By the way mum, you never have to work again."
Miller said his mum was a cleaner who suffered from arthritis, and all he wanted to do was "take those products out of her hands and give her the life she deserves".
Perry Como's It's Beginning to Look a Lot Like Christmas currently has almost 600 million streams on Spotify, while Michael Bublé's cover has more than 1.3 billion
The artist, who describes his style as "future-vintage pop", will join a host of singers who have covered It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas, including Bing Crosby and Michael Bublé.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge: Dafne Keen plays Greek goddess Artemis in season three, while Walker Scobell has starred as Percy Jackson since 2023
Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.
As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.
The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.
Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.
"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."
Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.
His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.
In an interview with Entertainment Weekly , external , he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.
Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".
"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."
Aryan Simhadri has previously spoken about an uncomfortable interaction with drunk fans
The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.
An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.
So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.
"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.
Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.
"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.
"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."
It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".
Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Annabeth, says Greek mythology offers "stories for everyone"
The first series was hugely successful with the opening episode of it reaching 13.3 million viewers, according to entertainment data company Luminate.
That dipped to just over 11 million for the second series and the cast is hoping a fresh take on the story will keep fans interested.
"I personally really like seeing people theorise about what's going to make it," says Simhadri.
"People who have read the books like talking about how they think we're going to adapt it, I love reading those."
It's been a big year for Greek mythology adaptations, with Christopher Nolan's blockbuster The Odyssey getting huge box office numbers and critical acclaim.
Leah Sava Jeffries, who plays Athena's daughter Annabeth Chase, says its popularity could be down to how people connect the ancient stories to their own lives.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvp8: The Strictly Come Dancing stage takes shape inside the historic Blackpool Tower Ballroom ahead of this weekend's live show
Long before the sequins start to sparkle under the lights and the judges prepare to lift their paddles to deliver their scores, Blackpool Tower Ballroom is a hive of activity.
I have arrived here before Strictly Come Dancing returns to our screens from the famous ballroom.
While instantly recognisable, the venue is very different from what BBC One viewers will see on Saturday night.
Instead of dancers taking to the floor, a team of production crew is taking over with a different kind of choreography.
Standing beneath the lighting rig, I find myself looking up rather than down at the famous dance floor. Above me are hundreds of lights, hoisted into position days before anyone steps on to the set.

It is only when I sit in the balcony that the scale of the operation becomes clear. Camera tracks snake across the room, crews move between rehearsals, and every few minutes somebody is testing a new cue.
Dozens of cameras, lighting rigs and crew members transform the ballroom into a live television studio ahead of the weekend's show
Blackpool week has become one of the most eagerly anticipated dates in the Strictly calendar.

Contestants spend weeks hoping they will survive long enough to perform beneath the ballroom's famous chandeliers, while fans look forward to the spectacular routines that the venue has become known for.
It's Olympic skeleton racing champion and Strictly contestant Tabby Stoecker's first time in Blackpool.
"Everyone has been describing the ballroom but I can't believe I get to dance in here," she says.
"I don't have words for this - it's so ornate and beautiful."
Fellow contestant Graeme Hall, also known as The Dog Father, says he has been "thinking of all the dancers who have been on this iconic floor, and now that'll be us on Saturday night".
Mirror balls hang from the ceiling of the Blackpool Tower Ballroom, ready to sparkle under the studio lights
While the spotlight is often on the celebrities and their journeys, Blackpool holds a special place in the hearts of the professional dancers.
Many of them hit the pinnacle of their competitive careers on this very floor.
Last year's Glitterball winner Carlos Gu says he "dreamt of coming to Blackpool every year since I was a kid in China - we heard about Blackpool before London".
He says: "Blackpool is the place where all dancers' dreams come true, it's a place that holds so many dance legends."
Fellow professional Lauren Oakley has an unusual claim to fame - she performed in Blackpool before she was born.
Oakley explains: "My mum won the British Championships in Blackpool when she was pregnant with me
"I can't count how many times I've been here - it holds so many memories and now it's nice to be here with Strictly."
Actor Jamie Winstone and professional dancer Carlos Gu pose backstage overlooking the Blackpool Tower Ballroom
The ballroom is a landmark in its own right, attracting visitors from around the world, but for one week each year it becomes the centre of one of the BBC's biggest shows.
By Saturday night, the cables will be hidden, the equipment will fade into the background and the focus will be firmly on the celebrities competing for a place in the next round.
But after seeing what is involved in bringing Strictly to Blackpool, it is very clear that the production off the dance floor is almost as impressive as what happens on it.
